prompt: Aristotle called metaphysics 'first philosophy' because:
options: It was written first among his works
It studies being as such, prior to all special sciences
It is the easiest branch of philosophy
It studies the physical world directly
correctAnswer: It studies being as such, prior to all special sciences
explanation: For Aristotle, first philosophy (what we call metaphysics) studies being qua being — the most general features of reality that all the special sciences presuppose. Physics studies moving physical things; mathematics studies quantity; but metaphysics asks what it means for anything at all to be. The name 'metaphysics' came later from Andronicus's editorial ordering, not from Aristotle himself.

prompt: Sartre's claim 'existence precedes essence' means that for humans:
options: Being is prior to knowing
We have no fixed nature — we create ourselves through choices
Existence is impossible without consciousness
Essence is identical to existence in God
correctAnswer: We have no fixed nature — we create ourselves through choices
explanation: Sartre reversed the traditional Aristotelian and theological view that things have a defining essence prior to existence (a chair's design precedes its manufacture). For humans, Sartre argued, we simply exist first and only acquire a character — an essence — through our free choices. There is no pre-given human nature constraining us. This is foundational for existentialist ethics and self-creation.

prompt: Kant's Copernican revolution in metaphysics held that the categories of understanding are:
options: Features of the external world we discover
Conditions the mind imposes on all possible experience
Derived from Aristotle's substance ontology
Grounded in theological truths
correctAnswer: Conditions the mind imposes on all possible experience
explanation: Kant argued that we never know things as they are 'in themselves' (noumena); we only know appearances (phenomena) as structured by the mind's own forms of intuition (space, time) and categories of understanding (causality, substance, etc.). This reversed the traditional assumption that metaphysics describes mind-independent reality, replacing it with a study of the conditions of possible experience.

prompt: Match each philosopher to their key metaphysical claim:

pairs.right: Reality is structured into substances bearing properties
Categories are forms of the mind, not features of reality
Humans have no fixed essence — existence precedes essence

explanation: These three represent major shifts in the history of metaphysics. Aristotle's substance ontology dominated Western philosophy for two millennia. Kant's critical turn redirected metaphysics inward, toward the conditions of experience. Sartre's existentialism radicalised the Kantian freedom thesis, eliminating human nature entirely. Each transformation built on and reacted to its predecessors.

prompt: Aquinas distinguished esse (existence) from essentia (essence) to argue that:
options: God and creatures are ontologically identical
In God alone are existence and essence identical; everything else is contingent
Essence is unknowable to finite minds
Existence is always prior to essence in all beings
correctAnswer: In God alone are existence and essence identical; everything else is contingent
explanation: Aquinas used the real distinction between essence and existence to mark the radical difference between God and creatures. Creatures have an essence (what they are) that is distinct from their existence (that they are) — they need not have existed; their existence is given by God. In God, by contrast, existence is identical to essence: God's very nature just is to exist. This underpins arguments from contingency such as the Third Way.

prompt: The Ship of Theseus puzzle illustrates the problem of:
options: Whether ships can be conscious
What makes a thing numerically identical over time as its parts change
Whether space and time are real
How causation works
correctAnswer: What makes a thing numerically identical over time as its parts change
explanation: The Ship of Theseus asks: if all parts of a ship are gradually replaced, is it still the same ship? And if the originals are reassembled, which is the real one? It probes what grounds numerical identity (being the very same thing, not just qualitatively similar) through change. This puzzle applies to organisms, persons, institutions, and rivers — anything that persists while its constituents change.

prompt: Locke's account of personal identity locates it in:
options: Continuity of the body and brain
Memory and psychological continuity
The soul as a non-physical substance
Social recognition by others
correctAnswer: Memory and psychological continuity
explanation: Locke held that personal identity consists in the continuity of consciousness — specifically, memory. You are the same person as your past self if you can remember their experiences. This divorces personal identity from bodily identity: a prince's consciousness in a cobbler's body makes the person the prince, not the cobbler. Critics (Reid, Butler) objected that memory presupposes personal identity and so cannot define it.

prompt: Parfit's view on personal identity in Reasons and Persons argues that:
options: Personal identity is all-or-nothing and must be preserved across time
What matters is not identity but psychological continuity, which can hold in degrees
Identity is determined by the continuity of the physical brain only
Persons don't exist — only bundles of events do
correctAnswer: What matters is not identity but psychological continuity, which can hold in degrees
explanation: Parfit argued that the question 'will it be me?' in hypothetical cases like teletransportation or fission may simply have no determinate answer — and that this doesn't matter, because what we really care about (psychological continuity and connectedness) can hold in degrees and branch. This had liberating implications: self-interested concerns become less rational if there is no deep metaphysical self to protect.

prompt: Match each theory about universals to its core claim:

pairs.right: Universals exist independently as abstract objects
Only particulars exist; universals are just words or concepts
Each property instance is an individual trope, not a shared universal

explanation: The problem of universals (why two red things share their redness) has generated three main camps since Plato. Platonic realists posit universals as genuinely existing entities. Nominalists deny any such entities — only words are general. Trope theory is a middle path: properties are real but each instance is numerically distinct (this redness is not the same entity as that redness, though qualitatively similar). Armstrong's immanent realism (universals exist in their instances) is another major variant.

prompt: Hume's bundle theory of the self claims that introspection reveals:
options: A simple, unified self underlying all experience
Only a succession of distinct perceptions with no persisting self
The soul as distinct from bodily experience
A stream of consciousness that guarantees personal identity
correctAnswer: Only a succession of distinct perceptions with no persisting self
explanation: Hume reported that when he entered most intimately into himself, he found 'a bundle or collection of different perceptions.' There was no persisting, unifying self — just perceptions following each other rapidly. Personal identity is a useful fiction the imagination imposes on this flux. This contrasts with Descartes (the cogito reveals a thinking self) and Locke (memory unifies the self). Kant agreed with Hume that there is no substantive self, but argued the unity of apperception (the 'I think') is a formal condition of experience.

prompt: The B-theory of time (eternalism) holds that:
options: Only the present moment exists
Past, present, and future are equally real in a four-dimensional block
Time flows objectively from past to future
The future does not yet exist
correctAnswer: Past, present, and future are equally real in a four-dimensional block
explanation: The B-theory (block universe, eternalism) treats all times as equally real — the distinction between past, present, and future is merely indexical, like 'here' vs 'there'. The universe is a four-dimensional spacetime manifold. This is favoured by special relativity, which shows simultaneity is frame-relative and there is no absolute 'now'. Presentism, the strongest A-theory, says only the present is real, matching phenomenal experience better but struggling with relativity.

prompt: In modal logic, a 'necessary truth' is one that is:
options: Knowable without experience
True in all possible worlds
True only in the actual world
Derived from the categorical imperative
correctAnswer: True in all possible worlds
explanation: Necessity is standardly analysed using possible worlds: P is necessarily true if P holds in every possible world; P is possibly true if P holds in at least one possible world; P is contingently true if P holds in some but not all. 'All bachelors are unmarried' is necessary. 'Water boils at 100°C at sea level' is contingent (it could have had a different boiling point). Possible worlds semantics was developed by Kripke, Lewis, and Stalnaker.

prompt: Kripke argued that 'Water is H₂O' is an example of:
options: An a priori necessary truth
An a posteriori necessary truth discovered by science
An analytic statement true by definition
A contingent empirical generalisation
correctAnswer: An a posteriori necessary truth discovered by science
explanation: Kripke's great insight was that necessity and a priority come apart. 'Water is H₂O' was discovered empirically — it is a posteriori. Yet once discovered, it holds necessarily: water couldn't have been XYZ instead, because water is essentially H₂O. This was revolutionary because Kant had conflated necessity with a priority. Kripke showed there can be necessary truths knowable only through empirical investigation.

prompt: Match each theory of time or modality to its key claim:

pairs.right: Only the present moment is real
All times are equally real in a block universe
Possible worlds are concrete realities like the actual world

explanation: A-theory and B-theory divide the metaphysics of time; both have serious defenders. Modal realism (Lewis) is the most ontologically profligate theory of modality — possible worlds are as real as the actual world, just causally and spatiotemporally isolated. Actualism (Plantinga) takes possible worlds as abstract objects, reducing the ontological cost. All three positions have implications for free will, causation, and the nature of counterfactuals.

prompt: Kripke's concept of rigid designators holds that proper names:
options: Refer to whoever fits a description in each possible world
Refer to the same individual in every possible world in which that individual exists
Refer to mental concepts rather than external objects
Can be analysed as definite descriptions
correctAnswer: Refer to the same individual in every possible world in which that individual exists
explanation: Kripke attacked Russell's and Frege's view that names abbreviate descriptions. Rigid designators latch onto their referent directly, by an initial 'baptism' and causal chain — not via descriptions. 'Aristotle' picks out the same man in every possible world where he exists, even in worlds where he never taught Alexander. This had consequences for debates about essence, the mind-body problem, and the semantics of natural kind terms like 'water' and 'gold'.

prompt: Determinism, in the context of free will, holds that:
options: Every human choice is random
Every event including human decisions is causally necessitated by prior events and natural laws
Free will requires quantum indeterminacy
Moral responsibility is impossible
correctAnswer: Every event including human decisions is causally necessitated by prior events and natural laws
explanation: Determinism is the thesis that the complete physical state of the universe at any time, together with the laws of nature, fixes every subsequent state. If true, your 'choices' are the inevitable outputs of prior causes stretching back before your birth. The free will problem asks whether moral responsibility is possible under this condition. Determinism doesn't entail hard determinism — compatibilists accept both determinism and responsibility.

prompt: Compatibilism about free will holds that:
options: Free will and determinism are both false
Free will requires that determinism be false
Free will and determinism are logically compatible
Quantum mechanics guarantees free will
correctAnswer: Free will and determinism are logically compatible
explanation: Compatibilists argue that the kind of freedom required for moral responsibility — acting from one's own reasons and desires, without coercion or compulsion — is perfectly consistent with determinism. Even if my actions are causally determined, if they flow from my own values and reasoning (rather than external force or internal compulsion like addiction), I act freely. Hume, Hobbes, and more recently Frankfurt and Strawson are leading compatibilists.

prompt: Harry Frankfurt's cases involving a neuroscientist who would intervene if the agent chose otherwise are designed to show:
options: That determinism undermines moral responsibility
That 'could have done otherwise' is not necessary for moral responsibility
That quantum indeterminism grounds free will
That agent causation is philosophically coherent
correctAnswer: That 'could have done otherwise' is not necessary for moral responsibility
explanation: Frankfurt constructed cases where an agent cannot do otherwise (a neuroscientist would override any deviant choice) yet we still hold them responsible because they acted from their own reasons and the neuroscientist never intervened. This challenges the Principle of Alternative Possibilities (PAP): moral responsibility requires the ability to do otherwise. If Frankfurt cases succeed, PAP is false, and incompatibilist arguments that rely on it fail.

prompt: Match each free will position to its core stance:

pairs.right: Determinism is true; free will is illusory; moral responsibility fails
Free will and determinism are compatible; responsibility survives
Free will exists and requires that determinism be false

explanation: These are the three main positions in the free will debate. Hard determinism (Pereboom's 'hard incompatibilism') eliminates moral desert while still allowing forward-looking practices. Compatibilism (Hume, Frankfurt, Strawson) redefines free will in terms compatible with determinism. Libertarianism (Chisholm, Kane) insists on genuine agent causation or indeterminism. Each position faces serious objections; the debate remains among philosophy's most active.

prompt: P.F. Strawson's 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962) argued that moral responsibility is grounded in:
options: Libertarian agent causation
Metaphysical analysis of causation
Reactive attitudes like resentment and gratitude that are constitutive of personal relationships
The causal history of beliefs and desires
correctAnswer: Reactive attitudes like resentment and gratitude that are constitutive of personal relationships
explanation: Strawson took a pragmatic turn: instead of asking whether determinism permits responsibility in some metaphysical sense, he asked what our practice of holding responsible actually consists in. It consists in reactive attitudes — resentment when harmed, gratitude when helped, indignation on others' behalf. These are built into the participant stance of personal relationships. The question of determinism operates at a different level and cannot simply dissolve these attitudes.

prompt: Hume's analysis of causation concluded that we never observe:
options: Event sequences
The necessary connection between cause and effect — only regular succession
Physical objects directly
Our own mental states
correctAnswer: The necessary connection between cause and effect — only regular succession
explanation: Hume observed that we never perceive the 'must' in causation — only that events of type A are regularly followed by events of type B. The idea of necessary connection is a psychological habit (custom) the mind projects onto sequences. This was deeply influential, inspiring Kant's response (causality is a category of understanding) and generating the continuing philosophy of causation.

prompt: Lewis's counterfactual analysis of causation says C causes E iff:
options: C and E are both actual events
If C hadn't occurred, E wouldn't have occurred
C and E are connected by a causal chain of physical processes
C precedes E and E follows C in every possible world
correctAnswer: If C hadn't occurred, E wouldn't have occurred
explanation: Lewis analysed causation as counterfactual dependence: E depends on C iff had C not occurred, E would not have occurred (evaluated at close possible worlds). This captures much of our causal intuition — 'the short-circuit caused the fire' means: if there had been no short-circuit, there would have been no fire. The main challenge is overdetermination: if two fires simultaneously burn a barn, neither satisfies the counterfactual test, yet both seem to cause the burning.

prompt: The logical positivists declared metaphysical claims meaningless because they are:
options: False according to science
Neither empirically verifiable nor analytic truths
Too abstract to be useful
Derived from emotion rather than reason
correctAnswer: Neither empirically verifiable nor analytic truths
explanation: The Vienna Circle's verificationism held that meaningful statements are either analytically true (true by meaning, like 'all bachelors are unmarried') or empirically verifiable. Metaphysical claims like 'the Absolute is beyond space and time' or 'substance underlies appearance' fail both tests and are therefore meaningless — pseudo-statements expressing emotion at most. Carnap's 'Elimination of Metaphysics' (1932) is the classic statement. Quine later challenged verificationism itself, leading to a softer naturalism.

prompt: Jonathan Schaffer's 'priority monism' holds that:
options: The whole universe is the one fundamental object; its parts depend on it
All entities are equally fundamental
Only simples (mereological atoms) are fundamental
Grounding is a symmetrical relation
correctAnswer: The whole universe is the one fundamental object; its parts depend on it
explanation: Priority monism (Schaffer) claims that the whole cosmos is the fundamental entity; all parts are grounded in and ontologically dependent on the whole. This is opposed to priority pluralism, which holds that simples or a plurality of basic entities are fundamental. Schaffer draws on holism in quantum mechanics (entanglement makes the whole prior to the parts). Priority monism is distinct from existence monism (the view that only one thing exists), which Schaffer rejects.

prompt: Match each concept to its role in contemporary metaphysics:

pairs.right: Non-causal explanatory relation — what makes something the case
C causes E iff E would not have occurred without C
The whole universe is the single fundamental entity

explanation: These concepts represent the cutting edge of analytic metaphysics. Grounding replaced earlier talk of 'supervenience' and 'reduction' as the key explanatory relation in ontology. Lewis's counterfactual theory of causation remains the dominant framework despite objections. Priority monism is Schaffer's revival of Spinozistic holism using tools from formal ontology and physics. Together they show metaphysics as a rigorous, ongoing discipline.
